newsitem.title: USA: U.S. civil rights groups end Texaco boycott.
newsitem.headline: U.S. civil rights groups end Texaco boycott.

text.p: Saying Texaco Inc has changed its course, U.S. civil rights activists on Wednesday called off a consumer boycott of the oil company, which has been embroiled in allegations of racial discrimination.

"Texaco is on a journey from tragedy to triumph. The journey is incomplete, but they have changed their course," the Rev Jesse Jackson, flanked by other civil rights leaders, said at a news conference.
The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People also called off its campaign for stockholders to divest Texaco stock.

"The plan presented by Texaco today appears to be an effort that is a sufficient next step in dealing with the company's climate of racial insensitivity. As such, the NAACP sees no immediate need for a stock divestiture campaign at this time," NAACP president Kweisi Mfume said.
Civil rights advocates launched the consumer boycott of Texaco products last month, although the company settled a race bias suit for $176 million.

The settlement came amid a public outcry after plaintiffs' lawyers in the lawsuit against Texaco recieved secret tapes of senior executives discussing the destruction of damaging documents. The executives also allegedly made racist remarks.

"It took a combination of factors to trigger a review of Texaco's toxic culture -- worker resistance to indignity, the sacrifice of some jobs and careers, lawsuits, embarrassing tapes, a consumer boycott which affected Texaco's stock value," Jackson said.
He said the plan developed under Texaco Chief Executive Officer Peter Bijur would expand sales "by pursuing the urban market as opposed to the present strategy of urban abandonment."
"We are pleased Rev. Jackson is supportive of our program," a Texaco spokeswoman said, declining further comment.
While generally praising Texaco's plan to remedy discrimination complaints, Jackson said the plan had some shortcomings.
"Our standing concerns about the environment and further data remain unresolved," he said.

"Without detailed employment information on Latinos and Hispanics, without further details about African-American employment, without an adequate plan to reduce emissions of carcinogens, the plan remains flawed, and we'll continue to monitor and give adequate attention to these areas," he said.
